source: Kaelbling, Littman, Cassandra (1998) Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains
finding: Founding POMDP paper for AI. The agent keeps a belief state (a probability distribution over world states). This belief is a sufficient statistic for the whole history, so the process over beliefs is Markov.
numbers: Worked example: 4 states, start belief [0.333 0.333 0 0.333]; after EAST with no goal seen the belief is updated by Bayes rule and never reaches zero on non-goal states.
limits: Needs a correct transition and observation model; the belief is only as good as the model.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold state (hypotheses plus weights) can be treated as a belief; the full transcript need not be carried if the belief is kept right.
quote: comprise a sufficient statistic for the past history and initial belief state of the agent

source: Kaelbling et al. (1998) value function over beliefs
finding: Optimal t-step value over beliefs is the max over policy trees of linear functions of the belief, so the value function is piecewise linear and convex. Values are high in low-entropy beliefs and low in the middle of belief space.
numbers: With 2 states a belief is one number b(s1); with 3 states, two numbers. Each policy tree gives one linear function.
limits: Exact representation grows with the number of policy trees.
agent_relevance: Value of information is built in: gathering evidence pays only when the gain beats its cost (matches our S0 gate idea).

source: Kaelbling et al. (1998) tiger problem
finding: Tiger problem: two doors, LISTEN costs -1, correct door +10, tiger door -100. Listening is 85% accurate. Opening a door resets the problem to belief (0.5,0.5).
numbers: Rewards +10 / -100 / -1; listen accuracy 0.85/0.15; opening at random is worth (-100+10)/2 = -45 vs listen -1.
limits: Toy problem with 2 states.
agent_relevance: Canonical test of a stop rule: gather evidence until the belief is lopsided enough, then commit. BSE (2026) reuses it for an LLM.

source: Kaelbling et al. (1998) finite-horizon tiger policies
finding: The optimal 1-step policy opens a door only if the belief is lopsided, else listens. The optimal 2-step and 3-step policies from the uniform belief only LISTEN. The 2-step value function has five linear regions.
numbers: t=1: all three actions optimal for some belief; t=2: listen everywhere; five policy trees for t=2.
limits: Undiscounted finite horizon only.
agent_relevance: Optimal behaviour can be gather first even at short horizons; with budget left the agent should not commit early.
quote: it never chooses to act, only to listen

source: Kaelbling et al. (1998) witness algorithm and complexity
finding: Exact value iteration creates a set of vectors that can grow exponentially each step. The witness algorithm is polynomial in the size of the output sets but not in the worst case. Infinite-horizon value functions may have infinitely many segments unless the optimal policy is finitely transient.
numbers: Authors conjecture value iteration can solve all finitely transient POMDPs in finite time; not proven in the paper.
limits: Exact methods only feasible for tiny problems; approximation needed.
agent_relevance: Exact belief-space control is out of reach for an LLM; use approximate or structured beliefs.

source: Kaelbling et al. (1998) plan graphs
finding: The optimal infinite-horizon tiger policy can be drawn as a finite plan graph that picks actions with no explicit belief; graph position stands in for the belief.
numbers: Fig. 16 plan graph for tiger.
limits: Works when the policy is finitely transient.
agent_relevance: A fixed state machine (our S0-S9) can stand in for belief when the policy has finite structure.

source: Kaelbling, Littman, Moore (1996) Reinforcement learning: a survey
finding: States MDP basics: an optimal deterministic stationary policy exists in the discounted model (Bellman 1957). Value iteration stopping rule: if successive value functions differ by less than epsilon, the greedy policy is within 2*epsilon*gamma/(1-gamma) of optimal.
numbers: Per-iteration cost quadratic in states, linear in actions; iterations polynomial in 1/(1-gamma) at worst. Policy iteration is pseudopolynomial; worst-case iteration count open at the time.
limits: 1996 view; later work changed some open questions.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact stopping-bound idea: stop when improvement per step falls below a threshold tied to the discount.

source: Kaelbling, Littman, Moore (1996) partially observable section
finding: Calls partial observability perceptual aliasing or hidden state. The naive strategy of treating observations as states fails when different states look alike but need different actions (office-to-printer example).
numbers: Section 7.1 state-free deterministic policies; Fig. 9.
agent_relevance: Warns against acting on the surface cue as if it were the state.

source: Madani, Hanks, Condon (1999; journal 2003) On the undecidability of probabilistic planning and infinite-horizon POMDPs
finding: Policy existence for infinite-horizon partially observable MDPs is undecidable under discounted and undiscounted total reward, average reward and state-avoidance criteria. Answers an open question of Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis 1987.
limits: Seen only in search-result text, not the paper itself.
agent_relevance: Even approximate optimal control under hidden state has hard limits; use budgets and finite horizons.

source: Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis (1987) The complexity of Markov decision processes
finding: Cited by the Perseus paper as showing exact POMDP solving is intractable. Not opened this session.
numbers: Math. Oper. Res. 12(3) 441-450.
limits: Citation only, via the opened Perseus paper.
agent_relevance: Intractability result behind the move to approximate and online planners.

source: Pineau, Gordon, Thrun (2003) Point-based value iteration
finding: PBVI backs up only a fixed set of reachable belief points, one vector per point, and grows the set over time (anytime). Claims history size, not state count, drives cost: the curse of history beats the curse of dimensionality.
numbers: Tag domain: 870 states, 5 actions, 30 observations; Maze33 averaged over 151 runs; Hallway and Hallway2 over 251 runs; Tag over 10 runs x 100 start positions.
limits: Authors note times from other papers came from different platforms.
agent_relevance: Sampling reachable beliefs is the cheap way to plan; our agent need only track beliefs it can actually reach.
quote: if we can avoid the curse of history, there are many real-world POMDPs where the curse of dimensionality is not a problem

source: Pineau et al. (2003) Tag results and belief-selection rule
finding: On Tag, QMDP (assumes the state will be known next step) scored -16.769 and PBVI scored -9.180. The belief-point heuristic that targets error bounds (SSEA) did best on Tag; random exploration did worst.
numbers: Reward -16.769 (QMDP) vs -9.180 (PBVI). PBVI time appears as 180,880 s in the extracted table (layout garbled).
limits: Table extracted from PDF with merged columns; the time value is uncertain. The Perseus paper lists PBVI Tag time as 59,772 s.
agent_relevance: QMDP-style planning fails where information-gathering matters; supports explicit info-gathering states.
quote: it lacks the representational power to compute a good policy

source: Spaan and Vlassis (2005) Perseus: randomized point-based value iteration for POMDPs
finding: Backing up only a random subset of beliefs can still improve the value of all beliefs in the set, giving much smaller value functions and big speedups.
numbers: Tag, belief set 10,000: Perseus -6.17 with 280 vectors in 1,670 s; PBVI -9.18 with 940 vectors in 59,772 s (as quoted from Pineau); QMDP -16.9. 10 runs x 10 trajectories x 100 starts.
limits: Times come from different machines and publications.
agent_relevance: Cheap randomised improvement beats exhaustive update; suggests sparse revision, not full re-derivation each step.

source: Spaan and Vlassis (2005) Perseus on Hallway benchmarks
finding: On Hallway and Hallway2, Perseus matched PBVI and HSVI reward with far smaller value functions and times.
numbers: Hallway: Perseus 0.51 reward, 55 vectors, 35 s; PBVI 0.53, 86, 288 s; HSVI 0.52, 1341, 10,836 s. Hallway2: Perseus 0.35 in 10 s; HSVI 0.35 in 10,010 s; PBVI 0.34 in 360 s.
limits: Table layout garbled by PDF extraction; row labels inferred.
agent_relevance: Same quality at about 100x lower cost shows approximation is often enough.

source: Silver and Veness (2010) Monte-Carlo planning in large POMDPs (POMCP)
finding: POMCP runs Monte-Carlo tree search over histories, with an unweighted particle filter for the belief and only a black-box simulator. One set of simulations serves both search and belief update.
numbers: Beliefs of K particles; particle reinvigoration needed in large problems; discount 0.95 in rocksample and pocman.
limits: Needs a good simulator; UCT can be greedy.
agent_relevance: A simulator plus sampled hypotheses is a workable belief; an LLM could act as the simulator (see Tru-POMDP).

source: Silver and Veness (2010) rocksample results
finding: POMCP scaled beyond full-width planners. On RockSample(11,11) it matched SARSOP (1000 s offline) with 4 s online. RockSample(15,15) has over 7 million states.
limits: POMCP used prior knowledge (preferred actions); a later paper could not reproduce its scores.
agent_relevance: Search over beliefs roughly doubles the reward of rollout alone.

source: Silver and Veness (2010) battleship and pocman
finding: Battleship: 10x10 grid, about 10^18 states, 100 actions, 2 observations. POMCP sank all ships more than 50 moves faster than random and 25 moves faster than random among preferred actions. The search tree added only a little over PO-rollouts. Pocman has about 10^56 states.
numbers: Battleship: -1 per step, +100 terminal, gamma = 1. Pocman: -1 step, +10 pellet, +25 ghost, -100 death, gamma 0.95.
limits: Tree benefit small because action values differ little and returns are noisy.
agent_relevance: Where action values are close and noise is high, extra search buys little; use a stop rule.

source: Kurniawati, Hsu, Lee (2008) SARSOP: point-based POMDP planning by approximating optimally reachable belief spaces
finding: SARSOP samples near the optimally reachable belief space, a small subset of the reachable space, learned online. In five of six robot tasks it substantially beat HSVI2, sometimes by several times; on Tag and Integrated Exploration HSVI2 could not match it in two hours.
numbers: Six tasks, two-hour limit, 95% confidence intervals; e.g. Underwater Navigation |S|=2,653 reward 722.59+-1.30 in 72 s.
limits: Authors' own benchmark choices.
agent_relevance: Focus on beliefs an optimal policy would reach: a prune-to-what-matters rule.

source: Somani, Ye, Hsu, Lee (2013) DESPOT: online POMDP planning with regularization
finding: DESPOT searches a tree built from K sampled scenarios and penalises policy size (regularisation) to avoid overfitting to the sampled scenarios. Gives an output-sensitive bound; works if a small optimal policy exists.
numbers: Tested on Tag (870 states), LaserTag (4,830 states), RockSample (7,8)/(11,11)/(15,15), Pocman (about 10^56 states); discount 0.95.
limits: Regularisation did not help on RockSample, which is nearly deterministic.
agent_relevance: Overfitting to a few sampled scenarios is the same risk as G3 (fit to given examples); a size penalty is a matching remedy.
quote: avoids POMCP's extremely poor worst-case behavior by evaluating policies on a small number of sampled scenarios

source: Somani et al. (2013) POMCP reproduction attempt
finding: Partial failed replication: the authors ran the public POMCP code on their own machine and got poorer numbers than Silver and Veness reported, so they printed both sets.
numbers: Table 1 caption says they could not reproduce the earlier results; table columns are garbled in extraction so exact pairs are not recorded here.
limits: Cause unknown (code changes, hardware).
agent_relevance: Planner scores vary with implementation; do not trust one paper's absolute numbers.
quote: We could not reproduce the earlier published results

source: Hausknecht and Stone (2015) Deep recurrent Q-learning for partially observable MDPs
finding: Replacing the frame stack with an LSTM gives a learned belief-like memory from one frame. On 9 normal Atari games DRQN did about as well as DQN; better on Frostbite and Double Dunk, significantly worse on Beam Rider.
numbers: Flickering Pong: screen fully hidden with probability p=0.5. Significance by t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg, P=.05. Most Atari games are MDPs given the last 4 frames.
limits: DRQN gains are game-specific; no overall win on standard games.
agent_relevance: Recurrent memory helps only when history truly matters; do not add memory where state is already visible (supports G1 and section 4b).
quote: on average, DRQN does roughly as well DQN

source: Hausknecht and Stone (2015) MDP to POMDP generalization
finding: Trained on full-observation games and tested with flicker, both DRQN and DQN lose score, but DRQN keeps more of its original score at every flicker level.
numbers: Averaged over all 9 games as percentage of original score (Fig. 5).
limits: Exact percentages only in a figure, not read.
agent_relevance: Policies trained with memory degrade more gracefully when evidence goes missing.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Tru-POMDP
finding: An LLM builds a tree of hypotheses as particle beliefs; Bayesian filtering plus belief-tree search plans over them. It beat ReAct, Reflexion and LLM-MCTS in kitchen rearrangement under hidden objects and vague goals.
numbers: 300 tasks (100 each at 2, 3 and 4-8 target objects), 5 RoboCasa kitchens, step limits 25/30/35, 600 s planning cap, GPT-4.1 for all. ReAct and Reflexion under 20% success with 3+ unknown targets; prompt-augmented versions about 40%; LLM-MCTS exceeded the 10-minute limit on all tasks.
limits: Simulation only; exact Tru-POMDP success rates are in figures not read.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an explicit belief plus search beats reactive LLM prompting under hidden state.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Tru-POMDP ablations
finding: Removing any part hurt: single max-likelihood hypothesis, no Bayesian filter (planning time up to 3x), flat hypothesis list instead of the tree (worse than single hypothesis due to hallucination), random rollout policy, no belief-tree search (lowest reward).
numbers: Fig. 4 and 5 ablations, same 300 tasks.
limits: Numbers are in figures.
agent_relevance: A flat LLM-generated list of hypotheses was worse than one hypothesis: staged, structured elicitation matters.

source: Jiang, Ge, Cai, Song (2026) PABU: progress-aware belief update
finding: Learns a compact belief for LLM agents: predict progress since the last round and store only useful interactions. Beat full-history baselines on AgentGym.
numbers: 8 environments; average completion 81.0%, 23.9% above prior SOTA; average steps 9.5, a 26.9% reduction. GPT-4-turbo 55.9% with 14.2 steps; AgentLM-70B 24.0%.
limits: Trained on the same trajectories; benchmark-specific training, not zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Dropping task-irrelevant history helped accuracy and cost; consistent with state compression over full transcripts.

source: Chattopadhayay and Halder (2026) Belief-State Engine
finding: An outside Bayes filter keeps the posterior over a POMDP; the LLM sees only the posterior, not the log. Claims a sound Markov policy on the belief MDP. On Tiger, a natural-language belief tracker behaved exactly like a reactive LLM.
numbers: Tiger, gpt-4o temp 0.3, N=40 seeds: BSE 38/40 (95.0%) success, 1.45 listens, mean return 3.06 [-4.41, 8.24]; Reactive and NL-Tracker 32/40 (80.0%), return -12.00, zero listens.
limits: Single preprint, reduced evaluation (3 of 6 baselines, 3 of 10 ablations, N=40 not 300x3); authors call some results suggestive. Intervals overlap.
agent_relevance: A model-written belief did nothing; a program-computed posterior changed behaviour. Supports program decides, model fills slot.

source: Chattopadhayay and Halder (2026) BSE ablations and attack graph
finding: Without the observation update the belief stays at ln 2 and 23/25 episodes time out listening. Dropping the prediction step changed little. On the 64-state attack graph the three methods were statistically indistinguishable.
numbers: Ablations N=25 (table rows misaligned in extraction). Attack graph (K=6, |S|=64, N=40): return Reactive -5.40, BSE -2.80, NL-Tracker 7.87; BSE coverage 42.1% vs 32.5%.
limits: Overlapping intervals; effect not shown on the harder task.
agent_relevance: The benefit is shown only on a 2-state toy, not yet at scale.

source: Fang and Ke (2025) InfoSeeker: information seeking under partial observability
finding: The LLM plans actions to test its own model of the environment before revising plans. Gain is large when dynamics are perturbed, small in the basic setting.
numbers: 11 partially observable tasks, 100-step limit, Gemini Flash 2.0 and GPT-4o; claims 74% absolute gain over prior methods on the hardest benchmark; mix-color 84% (+8% over best baseline); miscalibrated robot arm 80% while the best baseline fell from 100% to 6%.
limits: Under review; baselines are ReAct, AdaPlanner and LLM3 variants only.
agent_relevance: Active information seeking is worth its steps when the environment differs from the model's assumptions (matches impasse-triggered checks).

source: Imran et al. (2025) Are LLM belief updates consistent with Bayes' theorem?
finding: Defines a Bayesian Coherence Coefficient (correlation of expected and observed credence updates). Pre-trained models update in the right direction more often as they grow.
numbers: 6,460 tuples, five model families; BCC above 0 for all, rising with scale (exception: GPT-2 XL vs Large); correlation with log parameter count r = 0.906, p < 1e-6.
limits: Pre-trained-only models; workshop paper; correlation with scale only.
agent_relevance: LLM updates are only partly Bayesian, so keep the arithmetic in code.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench
finding: Multi-turn belief trajectories vs Bayesian references across coin bias, recommender, social judgment and triage. Scaling helps latent inference and evidence accumulation, but the gain does not reliably reach downstream prediction.
numbers: Seven open-weight LLMs, 3B to 70B; four environments; adapted from the bookbag-and-poker-chip task.
limits: Open-weight models only; numbers in figures not read.
agent_relevance: Models can infer a hidden state yet fail to act on it rationally; supports separating belief tracking from action choice.

source: AAAI-26 ELSLLM, LLM as belief module (search snippet)
finding: Search-result text says it maps observation-action histories into embedding space so an LLM approximates belief updates for RL under POMDPs. Not opened; authors and details unverified.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: Possible further read in angle B.
